Good morning. I call to order the informal meeting of the Plenary to hear briefing on the UNAID Initiative. I would like to welcome you all here and our briefers joining us remotely. This is the 6th in our series of monthly briefings intended to keep the membership informed and to sustain the momentum as the UNAID Initiative advances. While we have already achieved tangible progress across all 3 workstreams, significant work remains on our reform agenda, and I urge the membership to stay engaged with what lies ahead. Today, we will hear an overall update on the UNAID initiative from Under-Secretary-General Guy Ryder, followed by briefings on 2 work packages: Work Package 14, Unified Service Roadmap and Work Package 27, Environment. As a first briefer, as in the last meetings, I have the honour to give the floor to Mr. Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy.

Thank you very much, Madam President, Excellencies. Thank you all again for joining us for today's briefing. As you've said, President, the 6th in this series of briefings, and I want to thank you for providing this space for our interactions. Since the Secretary-General's progress report in May, UNAID has entered its decisive phase. Between now and September in particular, the task is to turn proposals into decisions, and we must do that together. Some proposals will require your consideration. In others, it is the Secretary-General who has the authority to act. But in either case, the aim is the same: a UN system which is, as our slide shows, more disciplined in managing mandates, better in implementation of mandates, and clearer in reporting on impact. Now, in recent weeks, I think it's fair to say that much attention has focused on 2 potential mergers. and of course they matter, but they're not the whole of UNAID. Today, let us step back and look at 4 points of progress along this mandate-to-impact chain. I want to start first with greater discipline around mandates. Resolution 80/251 asks the Secretary-General to improve how he assigns implementation responsibilities on mandates, based on comparative and collaborative advantage. And we are taking a first step towards applying that discipline in the proposed Programme Budget for 2027. You might recall the heat map, as we called it, from last year's Mandate Implementation Review. It's on screen now. The darker areas showed where Secretariat entities cited the same resolution to justify their 2026 programmes, and hence at least the possibility of overlap or of duplication. So, on the basis of this evidence and the resolution, for 2027, we issued stronger guidance, and colleagues have worked diligently to remove outdated references and to sharpen their focus. And the result is on the next slide. There it is. The green areas mean improvement. They mean less overlap. And so you see that we are acting on some of the areas of concern which have arisen in the UNAT process. And to be clear on this subject, this is not about any assessment of the value of mandates. It's about how we manage them, how we implement them. It's about discipline in how we, in this case, implement the proposed programme budget. And I have to say this is precisely what the resolution asks us to do, and in July we will update mandates.un.org and offer briefings to the ad hoc working group so that you can see this and more progress yourselves as we move forward. But as the resolution also recognizes, discipline begins earlier, and that is when mandates are drafted. You asked for better support, and to improve our support in the 81st session, we've established a new central point of contact, and you can reach that at mandates@un.org. Then let me move on to the second, the better delivery phase. Once mandates are assigned, the question is whether the system delivers well on them, and that is why today's brief on the Unified Services Roadmap matters. Back-office services are delivery infrastructure. Finance, Human Resources, Administration, and ICT determine how reliably we support teams and clients. The new roadmap turns common needs into shared solutions. For the first time, we have a joint approach across the system, pillars, global and country operations. And here the point is not just about savings, it's about better quality. Faster support and more resources directed to the mandates that you set. Third, the greater programmatic coherence phase. The environmental work that we will introduce today shows that UNAID reaches beyond efficiency Where mandates, expertise and capacity are spread across the system, we need to work with you to bring them better together. This is what we are seeking to do. Fourth, stronger impact reporting. Member States need to know what the system has done and what difference it has made. As a first step, we will make the Secretary-General's reports clearer, more data-informed, and more user-friendly, including by combining reports or adapting frequency. And we will share a written note on this with the ad hoc working group on mandate implementation review tomorrow. And let me conclude, Madam President, by looking ahead. This briefing is part of a sequence through to September And the next one will take place on the 22nd of July. By then, we will also share more information briefs and reports by the Secretary-General, and we will also support you with better digital tools. I had the occasion to mention the transcripts.un.org in the ad hoc working group meeting on Friday. Please have a look at it. Try it. It makes it easier to follow the many meetings competing for our attention. And I would conclude with one request. Please engage and give your attention to the QCPR resolution which is now under development. It is your most immediate opportunity to advance several UNAT reforms at once across the system. from better country configurations to shared back-office services. And again, the thread across our work, I hope, is evident: discipline at the mandate stage, efficiency in delivery, coherence across programmes, and a better account of the difference that we do make. And that is the spirit in which I look forward to your guidance in today's discussion. Thank you, Madam President.

I thank the Under-Secretary-General for Policy. I now give the floor to Ms Catherine Pollard, Under-Secretary-General for the Department of Management, Strategy, Policy and Compliance, and Chair of the High-Level Committee on Management. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you, Madam President, Excellencies, dear colleagues. Thank you for this opportunity to brief you on progress with Work Package 14, the Unified Services Roadmap. Can we put up the slides, please? We are presenting this roadmap at a moment of real constraint for the UN System. Projected system-wide revenue is set to decline by 21% over the 3-year period to 2024 through 2027. The UN System workforce has already shrunk by 12% in a single year. 3 in 4 of the UN system entities expect that there will be further programmatic changes in 2026. Consequently, the Roadmap's intended goal is designing a leaner and more effective and resilient operational backbone for the UN system that can help it to continue to deliver on its mandate, even in times of increased pressure. Next slide. At the heart of the Roadmap are 2 organizing questions for every operational service. First, should a service remain entity-led, or should it move to a marketplace of approved providers, or is it mature enough to be consolidated under one or 2 providers? Secondly, Are services best delivered globally, or should a service be integrated locally through common back offices and country-level agreements? These are not new questions. In the past, the system built up substantial capacity to try and answer them. What was missing was not capability, but coherence. The Roadmap is what organizes that capacity into a single navigable architecture. The design of the Unified Services Roadmap, the USR, is not based on abstract choices, but rests on strong data evidence resulting from 2 complementary assessments: the High-Level Committee on Management's Framework, that prioritize 18 far-reaching efficiency initiatives based on impact and feasibility, and the Global Shared Services Feasibility Study led by the UNSDG Business Innovation Group. That evidence leads to one central conclusion: there is no single model that fits every service. The system needs a differentiated architecture. Where the operating model and global versus local delivery are matched and analyzed service by service. For the level of consolidation, 3 operating models are used. First, entity-led delivery. The services with a high policy specificity or limited shared service potential would stay within individual organizations. Secondly, a marketplace of providers. Services where flexibility matters are offered through a common entry point with multiple approved providers. And third, consolidation of high-volume standardized services delivered by one or two providers that generates measurable efficiency gain. Next slide. So, the first message that I would like you to take away is this: the Unified Services Roadmap is the management framework that, for the first time, brings together, under one architecture, what had previously been advancing on separate tracks. As to the scope, the far-reaching efficiency initiatives are time-bound, self-standing transformation projects with broad but voluntary participation. Global shared services are not time-bound, location-independent services provisioned globally, while common back offices instead are location-specific consolidations of local service provision. And we are doing this work in conjunction with the New Humanitarian Compact under Work Package 2, That is a proving ground for integrated services approaches. Models validated in complex humanitarian settings can then be scaled up across the wider UN system. Next slide. I can assure you that the USR is not prospective. Implementation is already underway across all 4 tracks. Among the far-reaching efficiency initiatives developed under HLCM, an artificial intelligence-powered language services project is advancing technical and policy solutions, and a system-wide ICT procurement initiative has completed negotiations on a major software contract, with further contracts expected by August 2026, And a new UN Systems Services Hub is fully operational, providing one-stop access to booking 20 operational services through online servicing. So, as you can see, the far-reaching efficiency initiatives are only one part of the roadmap. My colleague from the World Food Programme will speak to the Coordinated Supply Chain Initiative, in conjunction with the New Humanitarian Compact. And on the Global Shared Services, the co-chair from the Business Innovation Group, they have agreed to a 3-tiered operating model and launched implementation in 5 priority service areas. Also, under the BIG's work on common back offices, the self-starter approach is already generating momentum. Let me emphasize a key point on accountability. We are tracking progress and making sure that we are accountable across all 3 tracks through public dashboards that are available to you, the Member States, and all interested parties on an ongoing basis, not just through periodic reporting. Before closing, I would like to stress an important point which we should acknowledge. It is about what efficiency gains can and cannot do. The enabling functions, which are the administrative and operational functions that we are discussing today, represent only 12% of UN system expenditure. So gains in efficiencies will not offset declining resources. What they can do is free up funding and management attention so that entities can protect mandate delivery and programme impact. That is the practical reasoning and justification for this roadmap. Madam President, Excellencies, in summary, the roadmap translates the UN 80 ambition of a more coherent, united UN system into a practical and accountable plan. One that simplifies where complexity has grown, integrates where duplication persists, and frees up resources for the programmes that the UN system exists to deliver. Madam Chair, with your permission, I would hand over the floor to Ms. Sonja Leighton-Cohn, who is the Co-Chair of the Business Innovations Group, who will speak to the global and local perspective across services under the Roadmap.

I thank the Under-Secretary-General for the Department of Management, Strategy, Policy and Compliance. And as mentioned, I now give the floor to Ms. Sonja Leijon-Kohn, Deputy Executive Director of the United Nations Office of Project Services and Co-Chair of the Business Innovation Group. We will hear her remotely.

Thank you, Madam President. Next slide, please. Distinguished member states and colleagues, the Unified Services Roadmap is the UN system's evolution in responding to a question member states have been asking: where are the efficiencies and how will we know? Today, for the first time, we have evidence and data across the system And we have a framework to act on it. As USG Pollard has just outlined, the Work Package 14, where BIG leads jointly with HLCM, covers global and local services and their connections with enablers like mutual recognition. So let me take each in turn, starting with the global shared services. The UN system already has a significant shared services footprint. 24 global shared service centers, 4 regional service centers, and 18 antenna hubs. The global shared services feasibility study confirms what this footprint can deliver, and it also highlights how much we're still leaving on the table through fragmentation. The evidence is precise. For example, one transaction for non-staff contracting costs up to 80% less when delivered through consolidated market provision than when handled in-house. That is not a projection. This is the cost of the current system every day we do not act. Next slide, please. Here is what the data is also telling us. The efficiency gains from agency-to-agency transactions, that is where one UN entity genuinely buys from another, remain far below their potential. Entities we have found are willing to provide services, but they are far less willing to receive them or buy them from others. Member States can help change that. You have the leverage through bilateral engagement, through QCPR, through the expectations you set to ask your UN partners not just what services they offer, but which ones they actually use from others. And on the slide, you see the list of services on offer that are mature. Next slide, please. At the country level, the new self-starter common back office methodology gives UN country teams the flexibility to build shared back offices at their own pace, selecting locally relevant services with common premises as the catalyst and country governance as the foundation. The model operates on a clear principle: no gain for any service provider, no loss. Service providers are to recover costs. They do not generate revenue. Full cost transparency is mandatory before any MOU is signed, and the UN country team under the auspices of the resident coordinator governs collectively. Uganda, the Philippines, and Gabon are preparing for launching. A high-impact survey tool has identified 56 priority countries, 24 in humanitarian settings, 32 in development, where the gains are greatest. We are going to coordinate with the humanitarian cluster to bring efficiencies together across humanitarian and development. But opt-outs after commitment remain the biggest obstacle to scaling. An abrupt or an uncoordinated disengagement often leads to severe inefficiencies. We do ask member states to be active sponsors of this change, to signal directly to your UN country partners that self-starting CBOs are what you expect, because we need to ensure we optimize coordination and efficiency locally. Next slide, please. Mutual recognition is the connective tissue without which none of this scales. 36 of 37 UNSDG entities have now signed the commitment. Signing is not the challenge, applying it daily is. The newly formed Interagency Task Force on Mutual Recognition brings together legal, audit, and human resource experts. Because that is precisely where the daily friction resides. First priority has been mapping end-to-end HR processes to identify where bureaucracy blocks what should be routine, such as shared rosters or portability of background clearances. Mutual recognition, we believe, serves as the vital lubrication underpinning operational efficiency. The architecture is in place, the data is clear, the tools are ready. What we ask of you today is to champion the work at the country level and in your bilateral dialogues. United to deliver means exactly that. Thank you.

I thank the Deputy Executive Director of the United Nations Office of Project Services, also underlining the role and responsibilities and power of Member States in their functions in the different boards and agencies with regard to the Global Shared Services. I now give the floor to Mr. Karl Skou, Acting Executive Director of the World Food Programme. He is also joining us remotely.

Thank you, Madam President and Excellencies, distinguished colleagues. Very, very warm greetings from Rome, literally warm. It's really hot here in Europe. I have the honor to update on our efforts to integrate supply chains And also to build a stronger system of shared common services. And these key actions are under Work Package 14, closely linked to Work Package 2 as well. There has been excellent momentum really behind these reforms. Agencies are truly breaking down barriers, combining their strengths, and finding practical solutions to find the ways forward. When challenges erupt. The goal is clear. Together, we can stretch the resources further, strengthen also our distinct mandates, and deliver more impact for those people that we serve and for the governments and countries that we serve. And we are advancing quickly now from design to delivery, as the Secretary-General has really asked us to do. We have the emergency pilots and day-to-day operations are already showing what is possible when we replace this fragmented approach with a more integrated and system-wide model. It's quite exciting, and let me start really with the integrated supply chain approach, which I would say arguably is one of the most tangible and exciting opportunities now coming out of this UN reform effort, this UN reform agenda. It promises game-changing cost savings, really, and real impact gains because 70% of the humanitarian spend is supply chain related. So it is a massive opportunity here. The premise is simple. Agencies will come together and deliver as one, not as a new entity, but by drawing on the best supply chain services of the leading agencies that is already available. The more agencies that participate, the greater, of course, the economies of scale will be and the greater the savings, but most importantly, the impact of this project. The model is being coordinated, as you may know, by DOS, the Department of Operational Support, IOM, UNHCR, OCHA, UNICEF, and us at WFP. So together we are now rolling this out, and it's kind of a 3-pillar approach focused on one, the integration of our agency's global procurement capacity. Second, the global logistics, the freight forwarding. And also third, then the harmonized in-country logistics. Any agency that is able to share these delivery services are being included, and we're now fast-tracking this model, launching in 5 priority settings already by the end of August. It's Afghanistan, it's Haiti, it's Palestine, it's Somalia, and it's Sudan. These are obviously very complex humanitarian contexts, but it's also where the impact gains are the most urgently needed, given the needs and the constraints around funding. So our plan is that, you know, once we've launched this, we review the lessons learned from this initial phase, and then we should be ready to scale this model to additional humanitarian emergency settings in other countries by the end of this year. And eventually, we hope to have a model that can also serve non-humanitarian contexts, of course, on supply chain to bring this benefit to the full system. UN agencies have already been adopting this kind of concept, if you will, of an integrated supply chain approach, now on an ad hoc basis in other settings. For example, over the past few months, we have worked very closely together in a kind of a joint engagement with maritime carriers to avoid what we estimate to be around some $2 million in surcharges, these emergency surcharges that was put on maritime carriers during the Middle East crisis. And so we came together, we negotiated exceptions, and by that jointness, you know, we got better deals and we were able to avoid these surcharges. Another example is now our contribution in the Ebola response, where agencies have collaborated much faster and more efficiently by sharing the different essential tools available. And platforms for this overall humanitarian response led by WHO, like for example dashboards to track PPE levels. So, you know, we expect really to see quick and measurable efficiencies as this model now matures, and excited of course to come back to you and keep you updated and report on progress. With that, I turn to the UN System Service Hub, which is already operational. It was the kind of foundations of this was, you know, it was created after the UN@80 initiative called for our systems to— or for our system to scale up more common services. But it follows the success of what we had before, which was called the UN Booking Hub platform. That Booking Hub supported some 22 UN agencies. And generated more than $18 million in efficiencies in '25 alone. So there is huge potential because now with the UN Systems Service Hub, we are extending this approach across a broader range of services and really with the potential to deliver efficiencies at scale. It's currently operated by UNHCR, by DOS, and by WFP. It offers some 20 services. It includes vehicles, it includes travel, engineering, asset management, and disposal. So there's a whole long list or menu of services that is provided. And it's really a simple— it's a platform that supports a marketplace model. You know, it connects agencies that has, you know, established services that they can provide with demand for that service. on a webpage. And we expect that, you know, this also down the road will create opportunities to also consolidate services, to bring them together once, you know, we have generated traffic on this platform. The UN Fleet, for example, you know, is a proven example where services have been successfully consolidated. This fleet combines the vehicle leasing of WFP, but also UNHCR in more than 100 countries. And it's being used now and drawn upon by many, many agencies across the system. We estimate that it already has, you know, an annual saving of some $1.6 million just by agencies, programs, projects not having to do huge procurements of vehicles, but leasing them from this joint system. So we really invite other agencies also to join us. To use this platform offering their service to others, but also identify further opportunities to consolidate these services down the road. So, uh, colleagues, I will finish with 2 reflections. I, I think first, really, and along the lines what Sonja said, you know, these reform models are now voluntary, but we really need agencies to participate and to do so consistently if we are to really realize the full benefits and the full opportunities on this. So we look to member states, we look to governing bodies to make sure that this happens by encouraging agencies to participate in these shared models and really providing, I would say, the political and financial incentives for us to work this way, to come together in this way. And secondly, just to remind that the the new Humanitarian Compact is really a catalyst for broader reforms, and emergency settings and humanitarian settings are now the testing ground for these system-wide transformations. So moving forward, we will continue to build on what works. We will expand these approaches that reduce fragmentation and that we think will enable more cost efficiency. in this UN or integrated UN model, a model that directs more resources towards our programmes, towards our programme countries, towards the people that we serve and that are counting on us to stretch every resource as far as possible. With that, I conclude, and thank you very much for having invited us from Rome, Madam President. Thank you.

I thank the Acting Executive Director of the World Food Programme in Rome, and in full solidarity, we have also very high temperatures here today at the other side of the Atlantic. We are all in this together. I now give the floor to Ms. Inge Andersen, Executive Director of the United Nations Environment Programme, also joining us remotely.

Thank you very much, Madam President, and I'm joined by Simon Steele. Together we have been working on this. Simon Steele, of course, the head of UNFCCC. And while I'm speaking to you, Madam President, allow me to thank you for making the visit to Nairobi. Also, many thanks to the member states present. We have— we're very, very keen to hear the views from member states on the environment package. We have had 2 briefings in Nairobi, one in Bonn, and I had the opportunity to brief more generally on reforms in my earlier visits in March in New York. We'll go— I'll ask that the team in New York kindly brings up the slides. Thank you. And we'll go to the next slide, slide 2. And what I would like to say here is that this work package is derived, of course, from the Secretary-General's 2025 report, United to Deliver, which stated that environmental issues are growing in importance and environmental responsibilities are dispersed across UN entities. And therefore, Secretary-General said that we would undertake a thorough assessment of the current arrangement and make proposals for possible structural changes and program realignments on environmental issues. And that is therefore what we have been doing. So we will go to the next slide. And the co-chairs, as I mentioned, is Simon Steele and myself, and we have had a large number of UN agencies involved. And what we have tried to do is essentially to look at how can we strengthen the coherence, reduce fragmentation, improve delivery across the environmental work of the United Nations system. And fundamentally, we see this as an opportunity to work across to address the environmental crisis, the climate crisis, the nature and land loss crisis, and of course the pollution crisis that we are facing as a civilization. And the briefing that we are giving you today will provide an overview of the findings as well as the recommendations that are under consideration. The process has been a very inclusive one. In this work package, as I'm sure all the others have been. The breadth of participation means that we have findings and recommendations that carry cross-system, and this we're very happy about. They give it broad legitimacy, not just one or two agencies' views. And throughout this process, we've obviously had a chance to exchange with member states, as I mentioned. We briefed in UNEP here at our Committee of Permanent Representatives in April. again just the other week on the 19th of June, and Simon Steele briefed UNFCCC parties on the 16th of June. We'll go to the next slide. And the context is, you know, why this review? Well, as we know, the environment that we all depend on for our very own existence and well-being is under stress and is deteriorating. And environmental degradation impacts, yes, ecosystems, of course, But it very much also impacts human health and well-being. And you're now sitting in extreme heat in a number of locations. And we've seen temperatures go way above or significantly above 50 degrees. And in Pakistan and other settings, this is the new realities, but it's also impacting our economies and therefore sustainable development. And that impact therefore reaches far beyond just the environmental bubble or sphere. And it has become that broad issue for health, for economic development, for jobs, for food production, yes, for human rights, for peace and security, for migration, and so, so much more. And our UN environmental architecture as we know it has grown significantly since when UNEP was established in 1972 in the Stockholm Conference 54 years ago. It has become broad, deep, complex and, yes, somewhat fragmented across agencies, funds, and programs, multilateral environmental agencies, and specialized organizations. So, next slide, kindly. What are then the findings? We're going to present sort of 4 streams of findings. The first slide here deals with 2 such streams, and we looked first at the science, governance, and 2 other streams. Allow me to speak to each stream. The Package 27, in the science side, we looked at the fact that science is produced on a number of beams. We know of IPCC, of course. We know, I think, of IPBES, which is the sister to IPCC, but deals with biodiversity and land degradation. And there is a new panel that deals with science, the science of pollution, waste, and chemicals. But there is more to that in the UN system. Our friends in UNESCO, as an example, deals with ocean science, and I could go on. So how can we ensure that the science that rests in different agencies across, that touches upon or deals directly with environment, is somehow united. And that is an area that we have talked a lot about, and there are some specific proposals in this regard. On governance, the abbreviation MEA, that is an abbreviation we use in the environmental space. It stands for Multilateral Environmental Agreements. There is a multitude of these. 17 such agreements are hosted with UNEP, but UNFCCC and UN Desertification Convention are also that, as are many, a series of others, BB&J being a case in point. These are multilateral agreements in a landscape that is complex, and there is a degree of overlap, a degree of synergy, and a degree of gaps across some of these mandates. And the multilateral environmental agreements really have the potential to improve the coherence through stronger coordination, administrative and programmatic synergies, program of work synchronization, and so on. In addition to that, we also believe on the governance side that UNEA, the conference that you have established, the assembly that is the only universal assembly that deals with the broad span of environmental policy, the Assembly of off the sort of conveyor belt of which most of the environmental policies and governance that you know of has rolled. But we believe still that it could be realizing its full potential as that universal body by some tweaks to how it operates. We'll go to the next slide where the other 2 streams of findings will be presented, and that deals with coordination and implementation. First, on implementation and coordination. On the coordination side, there is the Environmental Management Group, which was established by a UN resolution in 1999, a group that is about 50 agencies. The head of UNEP is the chair of that group. But that group could also be increased in terms of its role that it plays. It could be reporting to UNEA or to UNGA and to the Secretary-General. There are a number of opportunities. It could be using digital and interagency tools. It could create AI-enabled support centers. It could— or it could not create, but it could work take information from some of these new ideas that are coming out. The Environmental Management Group brings together these 50 agencies and works on topics that are topical and relevant. For example, the issue of plastic pollution. How can each agency from ICAO and aviation through agriculture, WFP and FAO and IFAD, through WHO, deal with plastic and the elements around plastic pollution. So taking that common approach across all agencies, but how can we go the last mile and provide the real technical expertise to agencies as they set about to do that? Some of the key cross-cutting findings, therefore, is that the challenge is not about the absence of institutions, but weak alignment amongst them. And so we feel that there's a real opportunity here to not work in these silos, but to find ways that we can have better MEA governance, better coordination across, and better work to ensure that the duplication and the siloing does not happen. We'll go to slide 7, please. So, what then are the work— this Work Package 27, what are the recommendations? There are currently 10 recommendations. And they fall into 3— under 3 global goals. And the next slide, please, slide 8. So the first goal deals with elevating the environment in the multilateral system. This goal has 4 recommendations, each targeting a different dimension. Recommendation 1 deals with recognizing that a healthy environment undergirds the UN Charter pillars. There can be— I mean, environment is a dimension of ensuring peace and security. Environment is a dimension of human rights. It is certainly a dimension of sustainable development. And each of these, when the environment is collapsing, chances are that there will be conflicts over water, over grazing, or whatever it might be. And of course, then it is not infrequent that human rights are infringed upon and that development is halted or stunted. So that's recommendation 1. Recommendation 2 speaks to UNEA as the universal environmental convening platform. This is nothing new, really. It is a role by which UNEA was established in the enabling UNGA resolution. So that is as it is. But Work Package 27 did find that UNEA has yet to realize that full potential as that universal body. Yes, All new treaties in the environmental space has, to a degree, as I said, been sort of cooked in UNEA or its predecessor. But there is more that UNEA could do to ensure a coherent and system-wide action. And calls, therefore, on member states are to consider how UNEA can move beyond deliberation to that system-wide agenda setting with stronger links to UNGA, to ECOSOC, and to the multilateral environmental agreements processes. The 3rd recommendation in this goal, under this goal, deals with repositioning science as a shared UN asset. We would like to seek a more systematic joint production of scientific assets that require across the system and across nexus areas through cooperation and collaboration. This recommendation also calls for more structured coordination amongst the key scientific and technical bodies and proposes what we call a federated knowledge ecosystem with a more modern user-driven repository of environmental science that is produced by UN entities so that these can be And today, with AI and good systems, this should not be impossible. And of course, for the systematization of UNEP's role, as well as other science-based UN entities, in developing environmental standards, benchmarks, and guidelines that promote alignment of other entities' programming, so that they take the meteorological sciences as it emerges from the WMO and put that to use in programmatic work. that they take the ocean-related science that emerges from UNESCO, or the science that emerges out of the 3 panels, IPCC, IPBES, and ISP, that it takes the science and is interpreted. And those who can best interpret it is, of course, the hosting entities of these relevant science bodies. Then recommendation 4 on elevating the environmental management group, ISP, spoke to that. The idea is really that it takes a greater profile, and it is— we believe that it is underutilized, and we propose a strategic upgrade, better connecting it to other coordination bodies across the UN, as well as to governing bodies such as UNEA and/or UNGA, and strengthen the exchanges as are already taking place at each COP process. and also have a direct reporting line to the Secretary-General. We'll go to the next slide, slide 9. And here we're discussing Goal B, the strengthened multilateral environmental governance. And this goal really addresses the architecture of the multilateral environmental agreement landscape itself. How do these agreements relate to each other, and can they work more efficiently in tandem? The recommendation 5 speaks to explore consolidation options where feasible. Now, I would just put a nota bene here. We're not talking about the big conventions, climate and so on. That should be self-evident. But there are many smaller conventions that nevertheless do important work, and consolidation is entirely doable. And We have some good experience already of this from the Chemical Convention, where 3 conventions came together, and therefore drawing on the successful experience from the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm Conventions, the recommendation explores whether member states might wish to consider opportunities for consolidation, for example, in the biodiversity space, where the adoption of the Kunming-Montréal Global Biodiversity Framework really has created an umbrella for action. So that would be one area that we think member states may wish to explore, or that of mercury, which has a standalone convention, which we think could potentially be considered to be drawn into the BRS, the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm conventions. So I will stop here now and hand over to my dear colleague Simon from who is speaking to you from Bonn, I believe, for him to take it further. Thank you.

Madam President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States, AOSIS. In this regard, proposals emerging from this process must be considered through a member-state-driven process. Madam President, allow me to highlight a few reflections on the proposed goals and recommendations. First, AOSIS welcomes the aim to elevate the environment in the multilateral system. Nonetheless, we would welcome further clarification regarding several of the recommendations presented. While AOSIS recognizes the value of UNEA as a universal convening platform, we emphasize that consideration of UNEA's role and functions should remain fully consistent with the mandate established by member states, including through UNEP's Governing Council Decision 27/2. In this context, AOC recalls General Assembly Resolution 55/198, which encourages the Conference of Parties and the Secretariats of the Rio Conventions and other multilateral environmental agreements, MEAs, and UNEP, including through the involvement of the Environmental Management Group, to continue enhancing complementarities among them. Importantly, such efforts must fully respect the status of the Secretariats of the Conventions and the decision-making prerogatives of the respective Conference of Parties. As such, AOSIS requests further details on the Environmental Management Group 2.0, specifically how this differs from the coordination functions already mandated to the current EMG. Second, on strengthening multilateral environmental governance, AOSIS recognizes the potential benefits of enhanced cooperation among MEAs where this can facilitate implementation and reduce burdens on parties, particularly SIDS. However, we recall that each MEA operates under distinct legal, institutional, and governance arrangements. They do not all share the same secretariat structures, administrative frameworks, and reporting requirements. Therefore, AOC stresses that any consideration of consolidation or enhanced synergies must be fully member-state-driven and respect autonomy, mandates, governance arrangement, and decision-making prerogatives of the governing bodies concerned. We would appreciate further clarifications regarding the recommendations relating to consolidating options, programmatic synergies, administrative synergies, and harmonized reporting, including how they would operate in a manner that fully respects the distinct institutional arrangements of the various MEAs without altering treaty-specific arrangements. Third, on scaling implementation of country commitments and priorities, AOSIS welcomes the focus on strengthening implementation support. For SIDS, the principal challenge is not a lack of commitments, but rather the persistent constraints related to finance, capacity building, technology transfer, and technical support. As such, we hope to see recommendations that address these particular challenges. In this context, regarding recommendation 8, What gap is the proposed coordination architecture intended to fill that is not already addressed by the MG? And how is it related to the proposed EMG 2.0? Further, if this coordination architecture is intended to coordinate implementation across MEAs, then further clarification will be needed regarding its governance arrangements, especially considering the existing authority of individual MEAs and within their respective governing bodies. We are also keen to learn more on the proposed creation of AI-enabled support centers. Specifically, how does the proposed climate support center relate to and avoid duplication with technology mechanisms under the UNFCCC, in particular the Climate Technology Center and Network? For AOSIS, it is important that we avoid the creation of parallel or overcomplicated structures That duplicate existing functions or arrangements under various MEAs. Any new tools should build on and strengthen existing mechanisms, remain party-driven, and support rather than fragment the current implementation support architecture. Lastly, on the next steps, EOSIS would appreciate further clarity on the timelines for and modalities for decision-making on each recommendation, as well as appropriate decision-making mechanism. Thank you. We look forward to receiving in greater detail more concrete information regarding these recommendations contained in this work package.

I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uzbekistan, followed by the United Kingdom. Uzbekistan.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. First of all, Uzbekistan expresses its full support for the ongoing UN 80 reform process led by the Secretary-General, aimed at building a stronger, more effective and efficient and responsive United Nations that is better equipped to deliver on the mandates entrusted to it by Member States. We thank the briefers for their informative presentations as well. Today's meeting provides an important opportunity for Member States to better understand the reform agenda, exchange views, and contribute to a transparent and inclusive process. We believe that a modern, coherent, and fit-for-purpose United Nations is essential to addressing today's interconnected global challenges. Regarding Work Package 14, Uzbekistan welcomes the efforts to strengthen coherence, reduce duplication, and ensure that more resources are directed towards programme implementation and support for countries. We appreciate the evidence-based and differentiated approach reflected in the Unified Service Roadmap. Reforms should remain flexible, responsive to different country contexts, and respectful of the mandates and comparative advantages of individual entities. We also support stronger country-level cooperation, including through common bank offices and other integrated service models, provided that they enhance efficiency and improve delivery on the ground. For Uzbekistan, operational reforms are not an end in themselves, but a means to enable the United Nations to better serve people and advance the implementation of the SDGs. Turning to Work Package 27, Uzbekistan welcomes the assessment undertaken and supports efforts to strengthen coordination, coherence, and effectiveness within the UN environmental architecture. For our country, environmental issues are directly linked to sustainable development and regional stability. The tragedy of the Aral Sea clearly demonstrates that environmental challenges require coordinated international action and strong support for affected countries. We therefore fully recognize that a healthy environmental— environment underpins peace, development, and human well-being. We support efforts to improve synergies across the UN system while respecting the mandates of existing institutions and multilateral environment agreements. Reforms should simplify access to support for member states, strengthen science-based policymaking, and harness innovation and modern technologies, including artificial intelligence. At the same time, national ownership and the country-specific priorities must remain at the center of all initiatives. Uzbekistan stands ready to contribute constructively to building a more coherent, effective, and impact-oriented environmental system within the United Nations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uzbekistan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you to the President and Under-Secretaries-General for your very helpful updates and amazing reform efforts. It's really very encouraging to hear the progress that has been made, and I agree with the representative from Cameroon that we need to keep focused. to really turbocharge this agenda this year. We support the Unified Services Roadmap, and we welcome the progress that has been made on Work Package 14. We think it's one of the furthest along under the UNAT initiative, and we also welcome the join-up with the Humanitarian Compact. It is critical that the Unified Services are truly system-wide, and that the UN specialized agencies and country offices are also bound into this. We would just like some greater clarity on the difference between the far-reaching efficiency initiatives and the global shared services. On Work Package 27, we also welcome progress on improving the UN environmental support. We would welcome more information on how these recommendations will be brought to life and what will be tangibly different. through them, particularly through the August briefing. We would also welcome greater delineation of which actions are for the Secretariat to take forward, or which require member state approval. That will help us prepare for discussions that are coming up at the annual subcommittee in September, and also any that might happen at UNGA High-Level Week. And then finally, we would like some greater clarity on the recommendation to establish a coordination architecture for the UN system-wide policy coherence and delivery in this area, and while we support the aim for better coherence, I think at this stage we don't necessarily agree that more structures will help to deliver that, so some greater clarity there would be helpful. So, you know, we continue to be committed to working with all of you to drive these reforms forward here and also via the posts that we have in various countries to achieve a more efficient, effective, and impactful UN, which can deliver better for people and planet. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste, which will be the last speaker of the day. Timor-Leste.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Timor-Leste aligned itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the Group of 77 and China, and by AOSIS. We thank all the briefers for the updates and we'd like to highlight the following points. Regarding the Work Package 14, Timor-Leste welcomes the Unified Services Roadmap and its objective of strengthening the effectiveness and efficiency of the United Nations system. We agree that no single operational delivery model can respond respond equally well to the diverse realities of Programme Countries. Greater coherence, reduced duplication, and more efficient service delivery should ultimately reinforce, not weaken, the Organization's ability to implement the mandate entrusted to it by Member States. We therefore support efforts to streamline operational functions, provided that the resulting efficiencies are translated into stronger support for country-level programmes. And development priorities. As the UNAIDS initiative advances, we believe the focus should increasingly include also how member states will ultimately assess the impact of these reforms. With respect to the environment work package, Stimulus believes that the success of any institutional reforms will ultimately depend on whether they better support countries in addressing the practical constraints that continue to impede implementation, particularly predictable financing, capacity building, and technology transfer. We look forward to continuing our constructive engagement with the Secretariat and the fellow Member States to help ensure that UNAID initiatives deliver practical, measurable, and lasting improvements in the United Nations' support to its Member States. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Team We have heard the last speaker of the day. I would now like to invite the briefers to respond. Now I would like to invite Ms. Catherine Pollard, Under-Secretary-General for the Department of Management Safety Policy and Compliance and Chair of the High-Level Committee on Management. Ms. Catherine Pollard.

Thank you, Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to all the distinguished delegations for your comments and your positive encouragement in this important work that, that we are doing. I'll just make some general points first before going to some of the specifics. The work that we are doing in the Unified Services Roadmap and in the Global Shared Services and common back office are all going to be within the existing mandates of the respective UN organizations. If there are any changes, or in terms of structures or how we deliver, then different organizations will have to go through their— the governance mechanisms within their individual organizations. speaking for the UN Secretariat. If there are going to be any changes, then we will put them— we will then go through the budgetary processes for which we have well-established procedures and where we fully engage Member States. So I just want to be very clear on that point and to reassure Member States. We are going to be using dashboards so that we can track the implementation, and those dashboards will also be made public so that member states have access to them. The idea is behind that, that you as member states will be able to hold us accountable to the commitments that we make to deliver. We will have the Unified Services Roadmap available by the end of June, as promised, and the full report by the end, by the end of October. Now, there were some, some specific questions. There were some specific questions. How would the work that we are doing in Workstream 3 under Work Package 31— just to go back to what I earlier said, we are continuing that work, and that is within the Secretariat. And if there are going to be any outcomes of those proposals that would then require changes in structures or functions, then we will present those through the budgetary proposals of the UN Secretariat for Member States to be able to review. There was a question about how do we plan to measure and report on achieved savings. that we are going to be using data, and we are going to track that through the centralized dashboards, as I mentioned. Those dashboards will consolidate the self-reporting. We will have regular updates from the various initiative leads, as well as the status on all— and milestones, and most importantly, the uptake on services. There was also— there's also a question about the technology platforms and whether we would be moving to have single technology platforms for services such as human resources and others in administration. The answer is not at this stage. There has been a lot of debate for a long time within the UN system about interoperabilities of ERP systems. That has been judged to not be feasible. However, what has been decided is that we will operate within the, the technology platforms that we currently have, that there will be 3 and 3 platforms where we have SAP, Oracle, and Workday, and as organizations do upgrades, then we will limit in terms of the variety of platforms that there are. That way, then we will be able to look at how we can better exchange data among the organizations. There was another question on how are the far-reaching efficiency initiatives different or related to the Global Shared Services. Now, the far-reaching efficiency initiatives and the GSS, they are linked, but they play different roles. The efficiency initiatives are time-bound. They are system-wide transformation projects, and they are designed to accelerate change in some of the priority areas. And they are innovative, and they are delivery vehicles, either test whether scaling or establishing new or improved shared service solutions across the UN system. By contrast, GSS are the steady-state delivery platform for shared services, and they provide ongoing location-independent operational services, such as, for instance, in human resources administration, finance administration, through either consolidated providers or market marketplace arrangements. I think I will stop there in the interest of time, Mr. President, because I know that other colleagues will have to speak. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Ms. Catherine Pollard and the Secretary-General. I now give the floor to Ms. Sonja Leijonkone, Deputy Executive Director, United Nations Office of Project Services, and Co-Chair of the Business Innovation Group. You have the floor.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. A couple of quick points to complement USG. Point one, I also want to thank all the very positive, supportive comments that we've received on the work package and the work going forward. And I wanted to confirm that we are using data efficiency tracking and engagement with resident coordinators to address bottlenecks or skepticism that may exist at local country level around efficiency gains or cost avoidance, but also to share how challenges can be overcome so that we make it easier to replicate. The second point is, I just wanted to reassure that notwithstanding the challenges we have had, it is gaining momentum. We can see it. Pakistan CBO is almost there. Zimbabwe has just formalized its commitment. We have others in various stages of interest and planning from the Philippines, Indonesia, India, Barbados, Colombia, Gabon, El Salvador, and many others. So, in terms of outreach, because there was a question around that, I mentioned briefly, but just to underscore, we have 56 countries that we have identified as high-impact countries that are being contacted to review their data and start discussing the processes to establish. And we also have a very active, supported with DCO support, process for peer connections. So, for example, Brazil could speak to Colombia because Brazil is an existing one. Gabon talks to Philippines. So we are creating bilateral synergies for learning and stronger multilateralism. On the concern that was raised by distinguished delegates about if self-paced is undermining urgency, Actually, thank you for raising that. We would like to clarify, actually, to the contrary, we have found that the approach that we've taken now with the self-starter has actually worked to fast-track and move quickly because it has gained relevance and political buy-in instead of it being what it was perceived as a top-down approach. It is now allowing the UN system to incentivize all the players at the local level and to engage as providers and recipients, and they also understand the cost drivers better. So that is something that's there. Final 2 points: Mutual Recognition is now working to determine the critical junctures in HR processes to create the one platform that the delegate from Libya mentioned, or the interoperability that Switzerland underlined, and to strike the balance of pace between urgency and accountability mentioned, as I heard, by Cameroon, G77, and EU. Finally, if I can conclude with a repeat of my call to member states to please engage and champion the work at the country level and bilateral dialogues. When you ask what you can do, It's very important that they know that this is something that is of significance and value. We also welcome if countries wish to consider appointing focal points in relevant ministries to support local UN country teams to champion the operational efficiency work at country level, that they can do so, and the RC would be the good entry point for that. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank Ms. Sonia Leighton-Conney, Deputy Executive Director. I now give the floor to Ms. Inga Andersen, Executive Director of the United Nations Environment Programme. Ms. Inga Andersen.

Thank you very much indeed, and first let me also thank Member States and distinguished delegates for the helpful comments that we have received. Allow me first to give some general comments and then to respond to a few specific questions and observations. Just to say that as UNEP, as the host of 17 multilateral environmental entities, agencies, excuse me, treaties, treaty bodies, we are acutely aware that those bodies and their COPs are the highest authority that could take any decisions pertaining to any convention. But that has not stopped in the past some of the conventions that UNEP has the privilege to host, for these conventions to engage precisely in a conversation about how they could consolidate. And so I mentioned to you here the Basel Convention that deals with illegal transboundary transport of hazardous waste. The Rotterdam Convention that deals with free prior and informed consent on hazardous waste, and the Stockholm Convention that deals with persistent organic pollutants. These 3 had separate secretariats, and then member states through the respective COPs took the decision to consolidate into one secretariat. And that is a precedence that stands, obviously it was not UNEP nor staff that took these decisions, but a lot of the engineering behind the works, obviously getting this convention secretariat into one, was supported by UNEP when Member States had so decided. So what we are saying is for some of the smaller conventions, there are real opportunities and very real cost savings that Member States may wish to consider. Far be it from us to say what they might be in terms of which could consolidate with what, but there are still opportunities in the biodiversity space and in the chemicals space. And we think that this is something that should be explored, and that is what the report would mention. But there's no doubt that the final decision lies with member states. And the same goes, of course, for uplifting UNEA and make UNEA come to its full promise. I think again here, having a conversation at the Next UNEA under the Jamaican presidency could be very interesting and something that I know that President Samuda, the president of the Next UNEA, is interested in. And on some of the specific points, Palau, on behalf of SIDS, OASIS. I mentioned about the clarification on consolidation options because indeed it belongs with member states. But there are also administrative synergies that are very real. We, UNEP, provide the IT, the HR, the procurement, and so on to these convention— 17 convention secretariats. Might we not be able to do that more efficiently by not having individualized actions in each of the secretariats? And the same for things such as those that Simon mentioned, Simon Steele mentioned, such as registration, etc., badges, and so on. There are platforms. It could just bring down costs and get greater efficiency. So these are some of the issues that we are putting forward. The same on the harmonized reporting. We've been working on harmonized reporting within the biodiversity-related conventions, and there are a fair number. Is there more that could be done here? I believe that there is. And when I meet with your national environmental counterparts and those that actually have to write these 20-odd reports, the burden is heavy. And I do believe that it's incumbent upon us to find ways that this burden can be lightened so that member states in the COPs can take decisions accordingly. But the analysis needs to be done by us because it's hard for 193 member states to do that analysis, obviously. But there's a big cry for that. On the Environmental Management Group, also a question brought by Palau. Just to recall, established in 1999 by the General Assembly, and it works to ensure the harmonization of understanding of environmental dimensions. Let's, for example, take plastic. The EMG decided 50 agencies to work on the issue of plastic pollution. Now UNICEF would deal with it from a children's angle, WHO from a health angle, ICAO from the angle of aviation, and so on and so forth. That is what the Environmental Management Group does. But there is a missing link. That link, when we have gotten the common approach to an issue, say plastic pollution, how does that then get delivered to the frontline of the country team? That is the missing link, and that is what EMG 2.0 will deliver because it's there that the reality needs to be delivered by the national authorities. So, it is not a new structure. It is enhancing and creating, crafting through the other work packages that missing link, so that the EMG can reach to the very frontline. On the next steps in the process, I think Simon mentioned that, but let me just say again, we will, as he reflected, in the next few days, seek to incorporate, strengthen our report to the Secretary-General. The Secretary-General will then incorporate what he wishes into his broader report, and beyond that, we expect that the Secretary-General might wish to issue a briefing, a brief, a small report in August that would consolidate his views for the next steps in the environmental reform package. It is clear, however, that yes, we will need to clarify in that package what kind of reforms belong on which side of the fence: COPs, UNEA, UNGA, other places, or indeed with the Secretary-General himself, or with various governance entities under the UN agencies. Ms. Andersen, I'm sorry to— Yes, thank you very much.

Thank you, thank you, thank you very much, Ms. Inge Andersen, Executive Director of United Nations Environment Programme. Now I would like to invite Mr. Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, followed by Mr. Guy Ryder. Mr. Simon Steele. I would also like to request the respondents to be short, precise, and because we have limited time available. Without taking much time myself, Mr. Simon, you have the floor.

Okay, I think I'll be as brief as possible. So, I just wanted to make 3 points building on Inga's comments. First, what we're hearing clearly is that there's— the issue is not about lack of mandates or initiatives, but it is that support of those mandates remains fragmented and not easy to access. So, the objective of Work Package 27 is practical, not political, and it is to improve coherence, reduce duplication, and make the UN system easier for countries to navigate. The second is to do with the support centres. These are not new institutions. It is building on what currently exists and making them work, making them work better. It is conceived as a networked demand-driven access function connecting what we already have. The third point is delivery to developing countries. The fundamental principle is about increased impact to developing countries on the ground, simpler access, more responsiveness, greater equity. And then there were requests about greater— the need for greater clarity and specificity and how this will work in practice. as we finalize the report, we will move from recommendations that have been put forward to some more concrete implementation pathways, which we believe will help member states better understand the direction that is proposed. And the comment, I think it was from the UK, is distinguishing between what decisions require member state decisions and what, in terms of coherence and better working arrangements, what decisions could be made within the respective secretariats. And then this point that constantly came across, it is to underscore the autonomy of mandates and the existing governance structures. and the nationally determined nature of member states' obligations and commitments. That is an absolute red line within the work that we're doing. And then the final point, I think the representative from Cameroon summed it up. This is about turbocharging delivery. This is about ensuring that the impact across the UN system is optimized and is as great as possible in a moment where there is need for urgent acceleration of implementation across the board. Thank you.
I thank Mr. Simon Steele, Executive Secretary of the UNFCCC. I now give the floor to Mr. Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy.

Thank you, Chair. I'll be very brief. Really, and above all, to thank Member States for their continued engagement, their encouragement, and their guidance today. And I think also, if I might add to that, the recognition that we are indeed advancing, and advancing importantly, in different areas of the UNAID initiative. Many of your interventions also have underlined the interaction, the linkages between different work packages under UNAID. And this, I think, also surfaces the underlying logic. It was set out in the Secretary-General's progress report of last month that drives UNAID, and as has just been said, if you skip over the ideas of efficiency, coherence, etc., it's about the impact that we can deliver for those that we serve, a shared objective that we can continue to work together upon. I was asked one specific question which I just want to respond to. Libya asked about the methodology underpinning those graphics I presented at the beginning showing the concentration of mandates in different areas. Just to be clear, this was a simple objective representation of the number of times that the same mandates are cited by multiple entities in their budgetary documentation. Suggestive, if not conclusive, evidence of overlap, not in the content of mandate, but in the manner in which the system manages those mandates. And we've been able to show how we're improving on that in the current budgetary process. And the second question put by Libya was about how we can assist member states in the formulation— formulation of mandates through templates, but indeed we're doing exactly that in the context of support to the working group currently working on mandates. That's all, Chair. A very encouraging session. Thank you to you all.

I thank Mr. Guy Ryder and the Secretary-General for Policy for his responses. The informal meeting of the Plenary is now concluded. I thank the delegations for their participation in the briefing and the briefers for their briefing. The meeting is adjourned.
